title: Neck and Shoulder Self-Massage: A 5-Minute Desk Routine — cv.cm
description: Self-massage for a stiff neck and shoulders: where the tight muscles are, GB20 and GB21 locations, a tennis ball on the wall, a 5-minute routine and red flags.
h1: How do you massage your own neck and shoulders?
answer: Work on the muscles at the back and sides of the neck and on top of the shoulders, never the front of the neck. Use the fingertips of the opposite hand to knead the top of the shoulder, small circles under the base of the skull, and a tennis ball against a wall for the area beside the shoulder blade. Use medium pressure and 30 to 60 seconds per spot.

sections.h: Which muscles get tight, and where they are
body: A stiff neck and shoulders after desk work, phone use or driving usually involves a few muscle groups. In Chinese this is often called 肩颈 tension, and in Japan 肩こり (katakori). Knowing where these muscles are makes your self-massage more precise.

head: Muscle
Where it is
How to find it
rows: Upper trapezius
The thick band on top of the shoulder, from the side of the neck out to the shoulder tip
Reach across with the opposite hand and squeeze the top of the shoulder. The thick part you grab is this muscle.
Levator scapulae
From the side of the upper neck down to the inner top corner of the shoulder blade
Turn your head 45 degrees to one side and look down. Feel the cord-like muscle on the back of the neck on the opposite side, just above the shoulder blade.
Suboccipitals
Small muscles just below the base of the skull, on both sides of the center
Place your fingertips at the bony ridge of the skull at the back, then slide down about 1 cm into the soft area.
Muscles beside the shoulder blade
Between the inner edge of the shoulder blade and the spine
Too far to reach well with the hands. Use a ball against a wall.

body.note: Stay on the back and sides of the neck. Do not press the front of the neck, where the large arteries and the windpipe are, and do not press directly on the bones of the spine.

sections.h: Two acupressure points: GB20 and GB21
body: In traditional Chinese medicine, two points in this area are often used for neck and shoulder tension. The locations below follow the WHO Standard Acupuncture Point Locations in the Western Pacific Region (2008). One cun is about the width of your thumb at the knuckle. Meridians and qi are traditional concepts. Pressing these spots is simply a precise way to massage the muscles there.

head: Point
Standard location
How to find it
How to press
rows: Fengchi (`GB20`), Wind Pool
Below the occipital bone, in the hollow between the upper ends of the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles

Slide your thumbs up the back of the neck until they meet the base of the skull, then slide each thumb outward about two thumb-widths until it drops into the hollow between the two large neck muscles. It is level with the soft spot just under the bump at the center of the back of the skull. It often feels tender.
Both thumbs at once, pressing up and slightly in toward the skull, not toward the throat. Pressure 4 to 6 out of 10, hold 30 to 60 seconds, 2 to 3 rounds.
Jianjing (`GB21`), Shoulder Well
At the midpoint of the line between the spinous process of the seventh neck vertebra (C7) and the outer end of the acromion

C7 is the bump that sticks out most at the base of the neck when you bend your head forward. The acromion is the bony tip of the shoulder. The point is halfway between them, on the highest part of the shoulder muscle.
Use the middle three fingers of the opposite hand, press straight down, or pinch the muscle gently. Pressure 4 to 6, hold 30 to 60 seconds, one side at a time.

body.note: Traditional advice avoids firm pressure on `GB21` during pregnancy. If you are pregnant, ask your midwife or doctor before using acupressure, and use only light stroking on the shoulders.

body: Sit upright with both feet on the floor. Breathe slowly. Warmth helps: a warm shower or a warm towel on the shoulders for a few minutes beforehand can make the muscles easier to work.

ol: Shoulder squeeze: reach your right hand across to the top of your left shoulder. Grip the upper trapezius between the fingers and the heel of the hand. Squeeze for 2 seconds, release, and move 2 cm along. Work from the neck out to the shoulder tip and back.

Finger circles on the side of the neck: place two or three fingertips on the back of the neck, beside the spine but not on it. Make small slow circles, moving the skin over the muscle. Work from the base of the skull down to the shoulder.
Base of the skull: rest your elbows on the desk and drop your head slightly forward. Place your fingertips under the skull ridge on both sides and make small circles, then press into `GB20`.

Levator scapulae hook: turn your head away from the side you are working on. Hook the fingertips of the opposite hand over the top of the shoulder blade, near the neck, and hold gentle pressure while you slowly nod your head forward and back 5 times.

Tennis ball on the wall: stand with your back to a wall and place a tennis ball between the wall and the muscle beside your shoulder blade. Keep the ball off the spine. Bend your knees a little to roll it up and down slowly. Pause on a tender spot for 20 to 30 seconds.

body: Pressure guide: light moves only the skin, medium moves the muscle, firm goes deeper but stays comfortable. For the neck, stay at light to medium. The shoulders can take medium to firm. Discomfort that feels good is fine. Sharp, burning or tingling pain means stop.
Do this at your desk when you notice stiffness, or as a short break every 25 to 50 minutes of screen work. A timer helps you keep to the times, for example cv.cm's pomodoro.

head: Step
What to do
Time
rows: 1. Shoulder rolls
Roll both shoulders up, back and down slowly, 10 times.
2. Left shoulder squeeze
Right hand kneads the top of the left shoulder, neck to shoulder tip.
3. Right shoulder squeeze
Left hand kneads the top of the right shoulder.
4. Neck circles
Fingertips make small circles down both sides of the back of the neck.
5. `GB20` hold
Thumbs press up under the skull, 2 holds of 20 to 30 seconds.
6. `GB21` hold
Fingers press the top of each shoulder, 20 to 30 seconds per side.
7. Gentle stretch
Ear toward shoulder, hold 20 seconds each side, no bouncing.

body: Massage feels better when the neck also moves. The NHS advises gentle neck exercises and keeping active for neck pain, rather than holding the neck still. Move slowly, stay in a pain-free range, and stop if a stretch causes tingling.

ul: Side bend: drop your right ear toward your right shoulder. Hold 20 to 30 seconds. Repeat on the left.
Chin tuck: sit tall and slide your chin straight back, as if making a double chin. Hold 5 seconds, 5 times.
Turn: look over one shoulder as far as is comfortable, hold 10 seconds, then the other side.
Shoulder blade squeeze: pull the shoulder blades gently back and down, hold 5 seconds, 5 times.

body: Small changes at your desk may reduce how often the stiffness returns. Put the top of the screen at or slightly below eye level. Keep a laptop on a stand with a separate keyboard if you use it for hours. Hold your phone higher instead of bending your neck down. Rest your forearms on the desk or armrests so your shoulders are not lifted. Change position often: no posture is good if you hold it for hours.

NCCIH, the US government center for complementary health, says massage may help neck or shoulder pain, but the benefit may last only a short time. A 2024 systematic review update (Lee and colleagues) of 42 trials comparing massage with other treatments for neck pain found that results varied by comparison, and that the evidence was limited by small samples and a high risk of bias. Massage did not appear to increase minor side effects.

For acupressure on `GB20` and `GB21` specifically, research is small and of mixed quality. The honest view is that self-massage may help you feel looser and more relaxed for a while. It is not a treatment for a neck condition, and it works best combined with movement and regular breaks.

sections.h: Mistakes, red flags and when to see a doctor

ul: Pressing too hard: if your neck feels bruised the next day, halve the pressure and the time.
Working the same spot for minutes: keep to 30 to 60 seconds per spot, then move on.
Pressing the front or side-front of the neck: never press there. Work only behind the line of the ear.
Cracking or twisting the neck: do not force the neck to "pop". Stretch slowly instead.
Using a massage gun or hard tool on the neck: avoid it. On the top of the shoulders, use your hands, a soft ball, or a massage gun on its lowest speed, away from the neck.

body: Do not massage the area, and get medical advice, if you have a fresh injury, broken or infected skin, a rash or a fever. People taking blood thinners, people with a bleeding disorder, and people with osteoporosis should use light pressure only. Ask your doctor first if you have had recent neck or shoulder surgery or are in cancer care.

body.note: Get urgent medical help for: neck pain after a fall, car accident or other injury; a stiff neck with fever, a headache or a dislike of bright light (possible meningitis, call emergency services); numbness, tingling, weakness or coldness in an arm or hand; a sudden severe headache; or trouble walking, speaking or swallowing.

body: See a doctor if neck stiffness does not improve after a few weeks, if painkillers do not help, if the pain wakes you at night, or if you are worried about it.

faq.q: How do I get rid of a knot in my shoulder?
faq.a: Press the tender spot with your fingers or a tennis ball against a wall for 20 to 30 seconds at medium pressure, then move the shoulder gently. Repeat once or twice a day. If it lasts for weeks or comes with arm numbness, see a doctor.

faq.q: Is it safe to massage your own neck?
faq.a: Yes, for most adults, if you stay on the back and sides of the neck, use light to medium pressure and avoid the front of the neck and the spine itself. Stop if you feel tingling, dizziness or sharp pain.

faq.q: Should I use heat or ice for a stiff neck?
faq.a: The NHS suggests either a wrapped heat pack or a wrapped cold pack. Many people find heat before massage makes the muscles easier to work.

faq.q: Why do my shoulders get so tight at work?
faq.a: Holding the arms forward, the head bent toward a screen and the shoulders slightly raised for hours keeps these muscles working without a rest. Regular breaks, a higher screen and forearm support often help.

faq.q: How often should I massage my neck and shoulders?
faq.a: A 5-minute routine once or twice a day is enough for most people. Short regular sessions are better than one long, hard session.
